papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section I, Section II (II.A-B opening), Section III.F opening (QML), Section IV.A (trainability and barren plateaus), Section V and Section VI (outlook) read in full; application subsections III.A-E, optimizer and efficiency/accuracy details skimmed by heading only.
papers.what_it_is: Review of variational quantum algorithms: framework, applications, challenges (trainability, efficiency, accuracy) and prospects for near-term quantum advantage.

assertions.value: In a variational quantum algorithm a quantum computer estimates a cost function (or its gradient) and a classical optimizer trains the circuit parameters, keeping quantum circuit depth shallow.
quotes: The trademark of VQAs is that they use a quantum computer to estimate the cost function
This approach has the added advantage of keeping the quantum circuit depth shallow and hence mitigating noise
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitional description of the framework by the review authors.

assertions.value: In a barren plateau the partial derivatives of the cost vanish on average exponentially with system size, so exponentially large precision is needed to find a descent direction; the review cites the original proof for deep randomly initialized unstructured circuits.
quotes: the magnitude of its partial derivatives will be, on average, exponentially vanishing with the system size
where it was shown that deep unstructured parametrized quantum circuits exhibit BPs when randomly initialized
assertions.certainty_reason: Review restates a result proved in a cited work (McClean et al.); the review itself gives no proof.

assertions.value: Global cost functions exhibit barren plateaus, whereas local cost functions give gradients that vanish only polynomially in n provided circuit depth is at most logarithmic in n (shallow random layered ansatze).
quotes: local cost functions (when one compares objects at the single-qubit level), exhibit gradients which vanish polynomially in n so long as the circuit depth is at most logarithmic in n
assertions.certainty_reason: Review reports a cited analytic result and says it was numerically verified in cited works.

assertions.value: Quantum advantage for practical applications has not yet been realized; the review calls VQAs a leading candidate strategy, not a demonstrated one, and notes trainability, accuracy and efficiency challenges remain.
quotes: the true promise of quantum computers, speedup for practical applications, which is often called quantum advantage, has yet to be realized
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit statement of status by the authors as of the 2021 revision.

papers.what_it_is: Introduces the quantum convolutional neural network circuit model with O(log N) parameters and applies it to quantum phase recognition and quantum error correction optimization.

assertions.value: A QCNN classifying N-qubit input states is characterized by O(log N) parameters, a doubly exponential reduction versus a generic circuit-based classifier.
quotes: makes use of only O(log(N )) variational parameters for input sizes of N qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the fixed hyperparameter structure of the architecture; the paper states it without a separate theorem.

assertions.value: In simulation for a Z2xZ2 SPT phase, the QCNN reduces the number of input copies needed versus string order parameters by a factor that scales exponentially with QCNN depth in the numerically accessible regime (fit 1.73e^(0.28d)), limited by finite-size effects.
quotes: QCNN reduces sample complexity by a factor which scales exponentially with the
depth in numerically accessible regimes (inset)
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical matrix-product-state simulation at N=135 spins, not a proof; the scaling is only claimed within the accessible regime.

assertions.value: A QCNN with N=15 spins and depth 1 (1309 parameters), trained by gradient descent on 40 points along an exactly solvable line, reproduced the 2D phase diagram over the whole parameter regime in simulation.
assertions.anchor: Sec. Obtaining QCNN from Training Procedure, p.5-6; Fig. 4
quotes: we focus on a relatively small system with N = 15 spins and QCNN depth d = 1

this QCNN accurately reproduces the 2D phase diagram over the entire parameter regime, even though the model was trained only on samples from a set of solvable points which does not even cross the lower phase boundary
assertions.certainty_reason: Single small simulated system; the result is demonstrated, not proved, and uses classical simulation only.

assertions.value: In numerical optimization with 9 physical qubits and 126 parameters, a QCNN-derived QEC code outperformed the 9-qubit Shor code under a correlated two-qubit error model, where the Shor code did worse than no error correction.
quotes: because the Shor code is only guaranteed to correct arbitrary single-qubit errors, it performs even worse than using no error correction
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result for one small architecture and one assumed error model.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections II (model, state preparation, circuit decomposition, readout), noise and resource analysis, dropout, benchmark Section V and Conclusion read; gradient-derivation algebra in Section IV and circuit-architecture design details in Section III skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes a low-depth variational quantum classifier on amplitude-encoded inputs with poly-logarithmically many parameters, a gradient scheme, and simulated benchmarks.

assertions.value: The circuit-centric quantum classifier has a number of learnable parameters that is poly-logarithmic in the input dimension, because it uses amplitude encoding and a polynomial number of gates in the number of qubits.
quotes: This circuit architecture ensures that the number of learnable parameters is poly-logarithmic in the input dimension
assertions.certainty_reason: Property of the architecture by construction, stated in the abstract.

assertions.value: The parameter saving holds only for the model circuit; state preparation can cost a circuit linear in the number of features, so the authors advise lower-dimensional datasets until error correction exists.
quotes: can always be done with a circuit that is linear in the number of features in the input vector
Still, until error correction becomes a reality, it is therefore advisable to focus on lower-dimensional datasets
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit statement of a data-access assumption by the authors; they note structured data can lower the cost.

assertions.value: In simulation on six benchmark datasets the quantum classifier performed comparably to multilayer perceptrons that train many more parameters, but overfit SONAR and WINE, so regularization remains open.
quotes: the QC performs comparable with the MLP models that train a lot more parameters
An open question is therefore how to introduce other means of regularisation
assertions.certainty_reason: Preliminary classical simulations on small datasets; the authors themselves call them preliminary.

assertions.value: In simulation, 1% random parameter noise had a robust but non-trivial effect on test error (mean relative change 7%), while 10% noise caused large losses, so the model should be retrained after such a perturbation.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V.B parameter noise, Table I
quotes: The 1% parameter noise had a more pronounced, albeit fairly robust impact
the model should be best re-trained after such perturbation
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on two 8-qubit datasets (SEMEION, MNIST256) with random perturbations.

papers.what_it_is: 2014 review of quantum neural network proposals judged against three requirements, concluding none yet qualifies and proposing open quantum neural networks as an outlook.

assertions.value: As of 2014, none of the reviewed quantum neural network proposals fully satisfied the authors' three requirements (associative-memory input-output relation, neural computing mechanisms, consistency with quantum theory).
quotes: QNN research has not found a coherent approach yet and none of the competing ideas can fully claim to be a QNN model according to the requirements set here
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative judgment by the review authors against criteria they chose themselves, dated 2014.

assertions.value: The authors identify the core obstacle as the mismatch between the nonlinear dissipative dynamics of neural computation and the linear unitary dynamics of quantum computing.
quotes: the nonlinear dissipative dynamics of neural computation [1] are fundamentally different to the linear, unitary dynamics of quantum computing
The problem seems to lie in the above mentioned incompatibility between both dynamics
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued conceptually, not proved; the later variational-circuit literature sidesteps this framing.

assertions.value: Quantum associative memory models can in principle store exponentially many patterns, far more than a classical Hopfield network, but the algorithms need resources far beyond the quantum hardware of 2014 and are not QNNs in the strict sense.
quotes: theoretically able to store 2N patterns into a qubit system of dimension 2n + 2
However, the requirements of the algorithms proposed are still far beyond the status quo of current realisations of quantum computing
assertions.certainty_reason: Review summarizes cited work; capacity is theoretical and depends on idealized quantum memory algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors propose Open Quantum Neural Networks based on dissipative quantum computing as a possible way forward; this is a research direction, not a demonstrated model.
quotes: An outlook on possible ways forward is given, emphasizing the idea of Open Quantum Neural Networks based on dissipative quantum computing
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposal only; the paper says the dynamics of related tools are yet to be studied.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II (informal Theorems 1-3), Section III (experiments) and Section IV Outlook read in full; the supplemental proofs (Appendices C-G, about 100 pages) were located by theorem headings only, not read.
papers.what_it_is: Proves exponential reductions in the number of experiments needed when quantum data is stored and processed coherently, and demonstrates the effect on up to 40 Sycamore qubits.

assertions.value: There exists a distribution over n-qubit states and observables where conventional experiments need order 2^n experiments to predict the absolute value of one observable, while a constant number suffices when copies are held in quantum memory and processed jointly.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II Theorem 1, p.3; proof in Appendix D
quotes: we prove that predicting just the absolute value of one observable requires exponentially many copies in the conventional scenario
while a constant number of experiments suffice in the quantum-enhanced scenario
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a theorem with proof in the supplement (proof not read here); depends on a quantum memory and coherent multi-copy processing.

assertions.value: Quantum PCA needs order 2^(n/2) conventional experiments but constant quantum-enhanced experiments; the authors state this does not contradict classical polynomial-time quantum PCA results because those assume entry access to exponential precision.
quotes: Here, we rigorously establish the exponential quantum advantage for performing quantum PCA
Those works assume the ability to access any entry of the exponentially large matrix
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem with supplemental proof (not read); the advantage is against conventional experiments, not against classical algorithms with sampling access.

assertions.value: A quantum machine can learn an approximate model of any polynomial-time quantum process from a polynomial number of experiments, while the conventional scenario needs order 2^n experiments for some such processes.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II Theorem 3, p.3-4; Appendix F
quotes: a quantum machine can learn an approximate model of any polynomial-time quantum process
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem with proof in the supplement (not read); requires coherent access to the process and quantum memory.

assertions.value: Experiments with up to 40 superconducting qubits and 1300 gates showed a substantial quantum advantage despite noise, but the quantum data was prepared directly inside the processor because no suitable sensors or transducers exist yet.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Sec. III, p.4-5; Sec. IV, p.6
quotes: we demonstrate that a substantial quantum advantage can be realized using
in which quantum data is directly planted in our quantum processor
assertions.certainty_reason: Experimental result on one device; the learning tasks are physical-state tasks with the state generated on chip, not a data-access-free setting.

papers.what_it_is: Technical note proposing an identity-block parameter initialization to avoid barren plateaus at the start of training, with numerical tests on a QNN classifier and a VQE.

assertions.value: The proposed initialization randomly picks some parameters and sets the rest so that the circuit is a sequence of shallow blocks that each evaluate to the identity, limiting the effective depth for the first parameter update.
quotes: The technique involves randomly selecting some of the initial parameter values, then choosing the remaining values so that the circuit is a sequence of shallow blocks that each evaluates to the identity
assertions.certainty_reason: Method description given in the abstract and Section 3.

assertions.value: In simulation (up to 12 qubits, 120 layers, 200 circuits per point) random initialization gave exponentially decaying gradient variance with qubit count, while identity-block initialization gave variance invariant to system size.
quotes: the variance decreased exponentially with the number of qubits, reproducing the plateau behaviour which was described in Ref. [1]
the variance of the circuit initialized as an identity block was invariant to the system size
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result on a limited range of qubit counts; the paper supports it with an argument, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state the initialization does not guarantee the algorithm stays away from the barren plateau after the first update; later training behavior is supported only by numerical results.
quotes: Obviously, this does not a priori guarantee that the algorithm stays far from the barren plateau
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit limitation stated by the authors.

assertions.value: A 10-qubit QNN classifier on binarized MNIST (132 layers, 200 trials) trained successfully in all trials with identity-block initialization and never met the plateau, and zero initialization trained poorly; the 7-qubit Heisenberg VQE showed the same pattern.
quotes: The circuit initialized using identity blocks trained successfully in all trials and never encountered the barren plateau
Similar to the MNIST experiment, setting all parameters to zero resulted in poor training compared to the identity block strategy
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiments on two small tasks; no hardware noise or shot noise considered.

papers.what_it_is: Proposes layerwise learning, which grows circuit depth during training and updates parameter subsets, and compares it with full-depth training under shot noise on MNIST 6-versus-9.

assertions.value: Under shot noise in simulation on MNIST six versus nine, layerwise learning attained on average 8% lower generalization error than standard training of an equal-size circuit, and up to 40% more runs reached lower test error.
quotes: layerwise learning attains an 8% lower generalization error on average in comparison to standard learning schemes for training quantum circuits of the same size
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation of one 8-qubit, 21-layer circuit with 100 runs per configuration and small shot counts.

assertions.value: LL reached accuracy above 0.65 with probability over 0.7, whereas every full-depth configuration had probability under 0.3, in 100-run experiments with 10 measurements per expectation value.
quotes: while LL reaches this accuracy with a probability of over 0.7 in both cases
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported from simulated runs with one random circuit instance and tuned learning rates.

assertions.value: LL and full-depth training perform similarly in noiseless simulation with exact gradients; LL outperforms on average only when realistic measurement sampling is included, and cuts repetitions to about half.
quotes: performance of LL and CDL strategies is similar when considering noiseless simulation and exact analytical gradients
reducing the number of overall experiment repetitions until convergence to roughly half of the repetitions needed by CDL
assertions.certainty_reason: Noiseless parity is shown in an appendix; sampling-noise advantage shown numerically for one setup.

assertions.value: The authors expect layerwise learning to help mostly with local cost functions, because global cost functions produce barren plateaus even in shallow circuits.
quotes: we expect that LL will mostly yield an advantage in combination with local cost functions
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an expectation based on cited barren-plateau results; not tested in this paper.
